item.title: A Practical Guide to Index Fund Dollar-Cost Averaging: From Valuation to Take-Profit
item.description:
1. Why Index Funds?

Dollar-cost averaging (DCA) is the best friend an ordinary person will ever have. The 10,000-hour rule does not apply in investing — choices matter 10,000 times more than effort.

1.1 Indices Are Immortal; Companies Die

Stocks come and go, but indices persist. Of the original S&P 500 constituents from 1957, only about 10% remain today — the rest were acquired or removed. Of the first 100 stocks on China’s ChiNext board, only 16 survive.

Indices have a strict self-cleansing mechanism: weak companies get kicked out, strong ones stay in. The index constantly renews itself.

An index is immortal; individual stocks are mortal.

1.2 Long-Term Annualized Returns Are Solid

Index Annualized Return (Including Reinvested Dividends)
S&P 500 ~10% (since inception)
CSI 300 ~9.2% (since 2004, with dividend reinvestment)
CSI 1000 ~11% (with dividend reinvestment)
ChiNext Index ~8.8%

1.3 Buffett’s 10-Year Bet

In 2007, a Wall Street fund manager challenged Warren Buffett to a 10-year, million-dollar bet: five top actively managed funds versus the S&P 500 index fund.

10 years later (2017), the results were in:

  • The five competing funds delivered annualized returns from 0.3% to 6.5% at best
  • The S&P 500 index fund returned 8.5% annualized
  • Every single active fund lost.

Buffett’s conclusion:

“By periodically investing in an index fund, the know-nothing investor can actually outperform most professional fund managers.”

1.4 Why Individual Stocks Are a Losing Game

Buying individual stocks means owning a slice of a single company and bearing extreme concentration risk. You need to answer: Is the company profitable? What is the P/E ratio? Is the business model sound? Are the financials reliable? What about management quality? Will the business become obsolete?

In the stock market, the real distribution is roughly 70% losers, 20% breaking even, and 10% winning. Most people who make money got lucky. Most people who lose money — that was inevitable.

2. Why Does DCA Work?

2.1 The Smile Curve

The essence of DCA: automatically buying more shares during market declines, thereby lowering your overall cost basis.

Consider this extreme real-world case:

On June 18, 2015, the CSI 300 stood near its all-time high. An investor began investing 2,000 yuan per month into a CSI 300 index fund — at the absolute peak of a bubble. By November 30, 2016, the index had crashed to 3,412 points. After 18 months of buying into a falling market, the total return was +8.58%.

How can you make money during a crash?

  • Early purchases were indeed underwater
  • But as prices dropped, the same 2,000 yuan bought more shares each month
  • The overall cost basis was dragged way down
  • It only took a modest recovery to turn profitable

2.2 Disciplined Contrarianism

When everyone else is panic-selling, you are DCA-ing. You know the index cannot die. You buy coldly, methodically. You might even start feeling good about getting cheaper shares.

DCA profits are, at their core, a reward for going against human nature.

2.3 DCA vs. Lump Sum

Method Advantages Disadvantages
DCA No market timing needed, smooths cost basis, disciplined Underperforms lump sum in a one-way bull market
Lump Sum Maximizes returns in a bull run Can mean years of losses if bought at the top

3. When to Start? — The Art of Valuation

3.1 The Key Metric: P/E Ratio

P/E (Price-to-Earnings) answers: how many years of earnings will it take to recoup your investment?

For an index, we look at the P/E historical percentile:

P/E Percentile Meaning Action
Below 40% Cheap Begin DCA
40%–80% Fair Hold, do not sell
Above 80% Expensive Prepare to sell

3.2 Tools for Checking Valuations

Tool How to Use
Qieman App Home → Market Temperature → Index Temperature
Xueqiu Fund App Home → Index Valuation → Check P/E percentile
THS (Tonghuashun) Search “Index Valuation Tool”
Rational Investor (lixingren.com) Professional valuation data
Ask an AI directly “What are the current P/E historical percentiles for major indices?”

When checking valuations, always look at 3-year, 5-year, and 10-year data to avoid being misled by short-term noise.

3.3 Special Note on ChiNext

ChiNext is more volatile. Check both P/E and P/B (Price-to-Book) to form a valuation judgment. Use the more conservative of the two.

4. Which Index to Choose?

4.1 Comparing Three Major Broad-Market Indices

Index Characteristics Volatility Best For
CSI 300 Large-cap blue chips, stable Low Conservative investors
CSI 500 Mid-cap growth Medium Balanced investors
ChiNext Small-cap high-growth, volatile High Return-seeking investors

Higher volatility means better DCA outcomes — you buy cheaper during drawdowns and rise faster during rallies.

Historical backtest (DCA from 2010 → sold at 2015 peak):

Index Total Return
ChiNext +185%
CSI 500 +120%
CSI 300 +63%

4.2 Don’t Put All Your Eggs in One Basket

China’s A-share market experiences structural bull runs — sometimes large caps rally, sometimes small caps do. Style rotation is the norm. Diversify across all three indices, adjusting proportions to fit your risk tolerance.

4.3 The Ultimate Lazy Option: S&P 500

If you want to skip the take-profit strategy entirely, pick an index with a persistently rising platform — the S&P 500.

  • US markets tend toward long bulls and short bears, trending northeast over decades
  • Even buying at the annual high every year yields ~10.6% annualized over 30 years
  • Buying at the annual low every year yields ~11.7%
  • The gap is narrow because the index’s floor keeps rising every year

Important: When buying S&P 500 QDII funds, watch out for premium rates and expense ratios. During periods of tight foreign exchange quotas, premiums can reach 30%, and subscriptions may be restricted.

4.4 A-Shares vs. US Stocks at a Glance

A-Shares (e.g. CSI 300) US Stocks (S&P 500)
Market Style High volatility, clear cycles Long bulls, short bears, rising floor
Must Take Profit? Yes — sell at high valuations Can hold indefinitely
Buy at annual high 5.63% annualized 10.6% annualized
Buy at annual low 10.69% annualized 11.7% annualized

5. How to Buy — Concrete Execution Plans

5.1 The Salaried Worker’s Plan (Simplest)

After payday each month:

  1. Deduct living expenses and essential spending
  2. Invest 70% of the remainder
  3. Buy weekly or monthly (over the long term, the day of the week makes no difference)

For a salaried worker, DCA is almost comically simple: paycheck arrives → subtract expenses → buy with the rest → done.

5.2 The Idle Cash Plan: Pyramid DCA Method

If you have a lump sum you won’t need for 3–5 years.

Allocation:

Use Share
Treasury bonds / reverse repos (ballast) 10%
Cash reserve (dry powder) 25%
DCA capital 65%

The Pyramid DCA Method (using a 3-year / 36-month cycle):

  1. Divide your DCA capital into 72 units (double the number of months, leaving room for accelerated buying)
  2. P/E percentile below 40% → buy 1 unit per month (narrow end of the pyramid)
  3. P/E percentile below 20% → buy 2 units per month (accelerate)
  4. P/E percentile below 1% → go bigger (extreme undervaluation, wide base of the pyramid)

Accelerated buying during crashes (if the market plunges right after you start):

  • 20% drop from peak → accelerate 3 months worth of purchases
  • 40% drop → deploy all remaining planned units immediately
  • Then resume normal monthly DCA

The index is immortal. You have no reason to panic. In fact, a crash should genuinely make you happy — shares just went on sale.

5.3 The Lazy Plan (S&P 500 Only)

No valuation checks. No take-profits. The only things to monitor are premium rates and expense ratios.

6. How to Sell — The Take-Profit Strategy

Selling is the hardest part. If you DCA into A-shares and fail to sell at the top, 3–5 years of disciplined investing will yield only mediocre results.

6.1 The 3331 Take-Profit Method

Valuation Point Action
P/E percentile hits 80% Automatically sell 30% of holdings
P/E percentile hits 90% Automatically sell another 30%
Approaches all-time highs Sell another 30%
Breaks through all-time highs Keep the final 10% — have some fun with it

6.2 Drawdown Protection

If the market stalls after reaching 80% or 90% percentiles and starts rolling over:

  • When it falls back to the 90% level, liquidate everything
  • Alternatively, leave the final 10% as observation

6.3 Only Take Certain Profits

When it is time to sell, sell decisively. We only take certain profits. The last frothy phase is for the final 10% — play with it lightly.

6.4 After You Liquidate

  • Spend a portion — reward yourself
  • Park the rest in treasury bonds or reverse repos
  • Patiently wait for the next undervaluation opportunity

7. The Power of Compound Interest

7.1 The Difference Across Annualized Returns

Starting with 1 million yuan at age 30:

Annualized Return At Age 60 (30 years) At Age 70 (40 years)
8% 10.06 million 21.72 million
10% 17.45 million 45.25 million
11% 22.89 million 65.00 million
15% 66.21 million 268 million

7.2 A 1% Gap Is Massive

A mere 1% difference in annualized return compounds into tens of millions over 40 years.

Beware of fees: over the long run, the gap between a 1.5% management fee and a 0.2% fee can eat up seven-figure sums. Always choose low-cost index funds.

7.3 Buffett’s Compounding Secret

Buffett’s formula is deceptively simple:

Longevity + high annualized returns = compounding magic.

The longer you live, the more ferocious the compounding in the later years. Start as early as possible — compound your knowledge and your money simultaneously.

8. What If Your DCA Is in the Red?

Losing money right after you start is completely normal. Here is the three-step mindset reset:

  1. Hit pause on DCA. Switch to reading mode. Thoroughly understand the principles.
  2. Rewire your thinking: when the index drops, you should feel happy — cheap shares are flooding in.
  3. If you truly cannot tolerate the drawdown, your understanding is not yet sufficient. Keep learning. Do not act emotionally.

9. The “Don’t Do” List

# Rule
1 Do not spend excessive time on investment research — when your capital is small, your time is best spent on career growth. That is where your fastest income gains will come from.
2 Never touch leverage, margin, or borrowed money for investing.
3 Never short the market.
4 Do not buy the top-10 performing funds of the past year (the champion’s curse — this year’s winner often becomes next year’s loser).
5 Never touch crude oil funds or commodity funds.
6 Do not go all-in — always maintain a margin of safety.
7 Do not act on emotion — don’t chase rallies, don’t panic-sell dips.
8 Do not abandon compounding — knowledge compounding and money compounding are the twin engines of financial freedom.

Any promise of high short-term returns carries extreme uncertainty. If you cannot bear the uncertainty of time, do not put money into a market that trades time for returns.

item.title: How to Pick Funds: The Seven-Step Framework
item.description:
The Core Insight: Funds Are Worth Holding for the Long Run

Top-tier funds can deliver 22%+ annualized returns over the long term. Yet nearly 40% of retail investors still lose money. The problem isn’t the funds themselves — it’s how you pick them and how long you hold them.

Funds have several structural advantages that are easy to overlook:

  • Even the weakest fund manager has an elite education and years of investment research experience — miles ahead of the average retail investor.
  • Every manager is backed by a professional research team with deep analytical capabilities.
  • If a manager underperforms, the fund company will replace them — a safety net that individual stock-pickers simply don’t have.
  • As long as you don’t lump-sum in at a bull-market peak, holding long-term means 95%+ of funds will eventually turn a profit.

Funds are not stocks. Do not trade them frequently. The tiered redemption fee structure exists precisely to incentivize long-term holding.

The Seven-Step Fund Selection Framework

Step 1: Ensure You Can Hold Long-Term

The first rule of fund investing is commit to holding long-term. The prerequisite: your invested capital must be idle money you won’t need anytime soon.

Avoid investing money that is:

  • Earmarked for a home purchase, tuition, or international travel within 1–2 months
  • Borrowed or leveraged
  • Your emergency fund

No matter how sound your investment philosophy may be, liquidity pressure will force you to sell at the worst possible moment.

Redemption fee tiers (for equity-heavy funds):

Holding Period Redemption Fee
< 7 days 1.50%
7 days ~ 1 year 0.50%
1 ~ 2 years 0.25%
> 2 years 0%

Zero fees after two years. This is the fund industry openly steering you toward long holding periods.

Step 2: Choose the Right Platform

Platform Type Pros Cons
Third-party platforms (Alipay, Tiantian, Qieman) Low fees, broad fund selection, fast settlement You need to do your own research
Commercial banks Personal service, simple process Extremely expensive (up to 10x third-party fees)
Direct from fund company Direct channel to the fund house Only that company’s products

Same fund, 1 million yuan invested: bank charges ~11,500 yuan in fees vs. ~1,000 yuan on Alipay — not even pocket change by comparison.

The verdict is clear: individual investors should default to third-party platforms. Fee differences compound over time — the money you save on fees is a meaningful source of returns in itself.

Step 3: Pick a Quality Fund Company

There is really one key metric: assets under management (AUM).

This isn’t an arbitrary number — it’s the result of investors voting with their feet:

  • Larger AUM → more management fee revenue → more resources to hire top managers and analysts → better performance → more inflows
  • It’s a virtuous flywheel

Public fund companies make their money primarily from management fees. Bigger firms have naturally deeper resources to invest in research infrastructure. Stick to major fund houses — your odds are simply better.

Step 4: Pick an Outstanding Fund Manager

Buying a fund is picking a manager. This is the single most important factor in your decision — bar none.

4.1 Years of Experience

The investment world is brutally unforgiving. Everything comes down to performance:

  • Incompetence or ethical issues → quickly eliminated by the market
  • Those who survive long-term do so because they’ve proven themselves
  • Longer tenure = richer experience = has lived through bull and bear cycles = better equipped for any market environment

An experienced driver may not be faster than a rookie, but they will definitely be steadier. In fund investing, steadiness matters far more than speed.

4.2 Track Record — Especially Drawdown Control

Don’t look at weekly or monthly returns. Don’t chase last year’s champions. Instead:

  • Zoom out: look for 3–5+ years of consistent profitability and disciplined drawdown control
  • A fund that doubles one year then halves the next is not an investment — it’s a rollercoaster gamble

The whole point of buying funds is stability. Whether you can hold on depends on whether the drawdowns exceed your comfort zone. Keep drawdowns within your tolerance, and you’ll be able to stay invested.

4.3 Job-Hopping Frequency

  • Strong performance + few job changes = high stability, a clear positive signal
  • Preference: managers who have spent most of their career at one firm → emotionally invested in the company → less tempted by distractions → consistently execute the firm’s investment philosophy

Many star public-fund managers are poached by private equity with massive pay packages. Those who “endure the quiet and guard their prime” are, by definition, acting in the best interests of their fund holders.

Step 5: Watch for the Right Fund Size

Size is the enemy of returns. This is an old saying in the investment world, and it holds true.

Size Range Potential Issues
Too large (tens or hundreds of billions) Hard to enter/exit positions, forced style drift, diluted alpha
Too small (sub-billion) Redemptions during downturns trigger forced selling → declining returns or even liquidation
Moderate (5–10 billion) ⭐ The sweet spot: flexibility plus economies of scale

Appropriate size is a bonus factor, not a dealbreaker. Zhang Kun delivered excellent returns at 100+ billion in AUM — though notably, he has since capped subscriptions, tacitly acknowledging that scale adds operational friction.

Step 6: Choose Diversified Funds

Spread your exposure across multiple themes and sectors.

Sector rotation is an enduring feature of the A-share market, and theme-chasing is hard to resist:

  • Single-theme funds: explosive returns when their sector is in favor; devastating drawdowns when it isn’t
  • Diversified funds: exposure across healthcare, consumer, tech, and more → far better drawdown control → a smoother ride for investors

Case in point: Zhang Kun (diversified across healthcare, consumer, and tech — steady drawdown profile) versus single-sector funds (all-in on semiconductors — wild volatility). Investors in the former almost certainly sleep better at night.

Step 7: Buy Old Funds, Not New Ones

Dimension New Fund Established Fund
Track record No history — marketing materials only Full historical performance, verifiable
Build-up period 3–6 months to deploy capital; will miss a bull run Fully deployed, in sync with the market
NAV Starts at 1, “looks cheap” May be much higher, “looks expensive”
Front-running risk New fund likely buys into existing funds’ top holdings → effectively front-running them No such issue

A fund’s investment value has absolutely nothing to do with its NAV! A NAV of 1 does not mean “cheap” and a NAV of 5 does not mean “expensive.” Funds make money from the underlying stocks appreciating, not from buying fund shares “low and selling high.”

Case study: E Fund Competitive Advantage attracted 230 billion yuan in subscription orders on a single day, against a cap of 15 billion — a 6% allocation rate. This tells you just how fundamentally most investors misunderstand how funds work.

Quick Reference: The Seven Steps at a Glance 

1
2
3
4
5
6
7

① Hold Long-Term      → Idle money only; no borrowing, no leverage
② Pick the Platform   → Third-party (Alipay, etc.); low fees
③ Pick the Company    → Large AUM = strong resources = deep research
④ Pick the Manager    → Long tenure + low drawdowns + stable career + through cycles
⑤ Right Size          → 5~10 billion is ideal; extremes on either end carry risk
⑥ Diversified Holdings → Multi-theme exposure; don't bet on a single sector
⑦ Old Over New        → Verifiable track record; no build-up period to miss rallies

Pro Tip: The Champion’s Curse

Never buy the top-10 funds by one-year return. This is a lesson the market has taught over and over.

In the history of China’s mutual fund industry, the previous year’s champion almost always suffers a massive drawdown the following year. Two reasons:

  1. Inflows dilute alpha: The championship year attracts a flood of capital, inflating AUM by orders of magnitude. The manager’s original strategy cannot scale to that level of capital.
  2. The champion was just in the right place at the right time: One explosive year does not prove a manager has genuine, repeatable alpha-generation ability. When the sector rotates away, the tide goes out — and you see who was swimming naked.

On Drawdowns and Volatility

  • Everyone calls you a genius when things are going up. Declines reveal who actually knows what they’re doing.
  • When evaluating a fund manager, drawdown control matters more than headline returns.
  • Extreme volatility → you will panic-sell → you will exit at the bottom → the subsequent recovery will not include you.

The ultimate goal of fund selection is not to find the fastest climber. It’s to find the one you can actually hold onto through the turbulence.

item.title: Investment Fund Basics: Stocks, Bonds, ETFs, and Mutual Funds
item.description:
Investment Fund Basics: Stocks, Bonds, ETFs, and Mutual Funds

When you buy a fund, what you are really buying is its underlying assets. A fund is only as good as what it holds.

1. The Three Foundational Assets: Stocks, Bonds, and Funds

1.1 What Is a Stock

A stock = a fractional ownership stake in a company.

Once you own shares, there are two ways to make money:

Method Description
Dividends The company distributes part of its profits to shareholders
Capital gains Selling your shares to someone else at a higher price

Why would someone pay more for your shares? Because they expect the company to earn more and pay out more in the future. By selling, you are effectively cashing out that future expectation today.

A stock has never been a lottery ticket. Its price is the market’s collective judgment of the company’s future earning power. What you buy is a piece of ownership—not a number bouncing around on a screen.

1.2 What Is a Bond

A bond = a loan contract. You lend money to an issuer, who pays you interest on a regular schedule and returns the principal plus the final interest payment at maturity.

Bond Type Issuer Risk Level
Government bonds Sovereign state Virtually risk-free (principal and interest are almost certain)
Corporate bonds Companies Carry risk (the issuer may default)

Key concept: interest rates and bond prices move in opposite directions

  • When market rates fall → existing bonds with higher fixed coupons become more attractive → bond prices rise (good for bondholders)
  • When market rates rise → existing bonds with lower fixed coupons become less attractive → bond prices fall (bad for bondholders)

Duration: the weighted-average time it takes for a bond investor to receive all cash flows. The longer the duration, the more sensitive the bond price is to interest rate changes.

  • If you expect rates to fall → extend duration (favour long-term bonds for greater price gains)
  • If you expect rates to rise → shorten duration (favour short-term bonds to limit losses)

Yield to maturity vs. coupon rate: If you buy a bond with a face value of $100 and a 3% coupon for only $80, your yield to maturity is far higher than 3%—because you bought at a discount and will pocket both the coupon payments and the difference between the purchase price and face value at maturity.

1.3 What Is a Fund

A fund = pooled money, managed by a professional, invested collectively into stocks, bonds, gold, and other assets.

  • Actively managed funds: The manager actively times the market, picks stocks, and adjusts the portfolio. Performance hinges entirely on the manager’s skill.
  • Passive funds (index funds): The fund tracks a pre-defined portfolio (an index) and makes no subjective stock-picking decisions.

Key takeaway: The vast majority of actively managed funds underperform passive index funds over the long run. This is not an opinion—it is a statistical fact, and one that Warren Buffett validated with his famous ten-year, million-dollar bet.

2. A-Share Market Basics

2.1 What You Can Trade

Market Eligibility Daily Price Limit
A-share Main Board No threshold ±10%
STAR Market (SSE STAR) ¥500K in assets ±20%
Hong Kong stocks (H-shares) ¥500K in assets (via Stock Connect) No limit

How to trade: Brokerages act as intermediaries between investors and the exchange. You must open an account with a brokerage to participate.

2.2 Trading Costs (Friction)

Every buy or sell order incurs the following fees:

Fee When buying When selling
Stamp duty Not charged Charged (seller only)
Transfer fee Charged to both sides Charged to both sides
Brokerage commission Charged (¥5 minimum) Charged (¥5 minimum)

⚠️ Heads-up: the ¥5 minimum commission can significantly impact small trades. Avoid frequent trading—frictional costs will quietly eat away your returns.

2.3 A-Share Taxation

Tax Type Rule
Capital gains tax Not levied (profits from trading are not taxed)
Dividend tax Withheld upon dividend distribution; the longer your holding period, the lower the rate
Stamp duty Charged on the seller only, at the time of sale

2.4 Key Terms Cheat Sheet

Term Meaning
Open a position (开仓) Buy an asset to establish a holding
Hold a position (持仓) The assets you currently own
Close a position (平仓) Sell an asset to exit a holding
Position size (仓位) The proportion of total capital allocated to a given asset
Going long (做多) Buy an asset hoping to sell it later at a higher price
Short selling (做空) Borrow shares, sell them, then buy back at a lower price (requires ¥500K threshold)
One lot (一手) 100 shares—the minimum trading unit on the A-share market
Candlestick / K-line (K 线) A chart showing the opening, closing, high, and low prices for a given period

3. ETFs (Exchange-Traded Funds) vs. Mutual Funds

3.1 Exchange-Traded Funds (ETFs)

ETF = Exchange Traded Fund.

  • How to buy: Exactly like buying a stock—real-time trading through your brokerage app
  • Price: Determined by live matching of buy and sell orders on the exchange; may deviate from the fund’s net asset value (creating a premium or discount)
  • Fees: Extremely low. For example, a broad Shanghai Composite ETF can have a total expense ratio as low as 0.2% per year
  • Why so cheap: ETFs passively track an index—no manager actively trading, no need to manage cash flows from retail investors entering and exiting

Premium/Discount rate = (ETF market price − NAV) / NAV. A positive value means the ETF trades above its true value (premium); a negative value means it trades below (discount).

3.2 Mutual Funds (Off-Exchange Funds)

  • How to buy: Subscribe or redeem directly through platforms like Alipay or Tiantian Fund—not through exchange order matching
  • Confirmation time: If you subscribe on day T, your shares are confirmed on T+1
  • Fees: Generally higher than comparable ETFs
  • Why more expensive: Fund companies must actively manage cash flows from frequent retail subscriptions and redemptions, incurring higher operational costs

3.3 Side-by-Side Comparison

ETF (On-Exchange) Mutual Fund (Off-Exchange)
Trading method Real-time, like a stock Subscribe / redeem with the fund company
Speed Instant execution T+1 confirmation
Expense ratio Very low (~0.2% p.a.) Higher
Premium / Discount Possible Not applicable (traded at NAV)
Barrier to entry Requires a securities brokerage account Alipay / fund apps work fine

💡 Rule of thumb: Go with ETFs if you want the lowest fees and plan to hold long-term. Choose mutual funds if you prioritise convenience and small regular investments. Over decades, fee differences compound into significant return gaps.

4. Reverse Repo with Government Bonds

A short-term cash-management tool with risk anchored to short-dated government bonds and near-zero credit risk.

How it works:

  1. You lend your cash to the exchange
  2. The borrower pledges government bonds as collateral to the exchange
  3. At maturity, the exchange returns the bonds to the borrower, and you collect your principal plus interest
  4. If the borrower cannot repay, the exchange can liquidate the pledged bonds to cover the obligation

Safety: With government bonds as collateral, your principal is virtually risk-free. An ideal parking spot for idle cash.

Annualised reference return: roughly 1%–1.5% (slightly better than money-market funds like Yu’e Bao).

5. Investing vs. Speculating: The Fundamental Distinction

Benjamin Graham’s definition of investment: An investment operation is one which, upon thorough analysis, promises safety of principal and an adequate return. Operations not meeting these requirements are speculative.

The Investor’s Checklist

  • Does the company make money? How much? From what source?
  • How long can its profit growth be sustained?
  • What does the competitive landscape look like?
  • Is the current valuation reasonable?

The Speculator’s Playbook

  • Buying on a hunch—“I just feel like it’s going up”
  • Staring at candlestick charts, trying to divine answers from patterns
  • Chasing hot themes, swing-trading, timing the market
  • Frequent switching between tickers in pursuit of short-term spreads

A candlestick chart tells you exactly two things and nothing more:

  1. At what price the market currently values this company
  2. At what price the market has valued it in the past

That is all. Past prices do not influence future prices.

A Story Worth Reflecting On

Look at NVIDIA’s candlestick chart from 2020: a noticeable drawdown, a slow recovery, then a relentless march to new all-time highs. If all you saw was the chart, tripling your money might have felt like a clear signal to sell. But if you understood the company’s future growth story, you would not have sold—and NVIDIA went on to multiply many more times from that point.

If your only reason for selling is “it looks like it has gone up too much, it feels risky,” you may well miss a once-in-a-lifetime wealth-building opportunity.

6. What Risk Really Means

Academia defines risk as volatility (variance). But true risk is not how much a price fluctuates—it is the risk of permanent capital loss.

  • If a company’s competitive moat disappears, its earning power is destroyed, and its business model enters irreversible decline—no matter how calm the stock price looks, the risk is extreme
  • If a company has durable earning power and steadily growing free cash flow—even if the stock price whipsaws violently along the way, as long as you do not sell at the wrong moment, you will not suffer permanent capital loss

How to Weather Volatility

Strategy Description
Don’t go all-in Never bet your entire net worth on a single company—that is gambling
Position sizing Keep only ~10% of your portfolio in highly volatile names; the other 90% stays diversified
Keep powder dry Maintain a cash reserve so you have room to average down and correct mistakes

Your willingness to endure periods of zero return—or even paper losses—determines the level of return you can realistically aim for.

The road of investing is long. Get the fundamentals right first, and you will not be led around by market sentiment.

item.title: Fund Classification 101: The Three Armies, Nine Unit Types Framework
item.description:
Core insight: Every fund on the market, no matter how creatively named, fits into exactly three categories. Understanding this classification is the prerequisite for entering the market. Most people lose money not because they picked the wrong fund, but because they bought something they didn’t even understand.

Overview: A Personal Finance Account Is Essentially Three Armies

Army Allocation Role Core Mission
Supply Corps 10% ~ 20% Money Market Funds Ensure liquidity — accessible anytime, almost zero loss
Imperial Guard 50% ~ 70% Bond Funds / Fixed Income+ Park 1–3 year idle cash, tolerate minor drawdowns
Shock Troops 10% ~ 40% Equity / Index Funds Park 3–5+ year idle cash, pursue high returns

Once you understand the division of labor among these three armies, you are already ahead of 80% of retail investors. Let’s break down each army’s unit types one by one.

First Army: Supply Corps (10% ~ 20% Allocation)

Its mission is not to generate returns — it is to secure your logistics. Park 1–3 months of living expenses and emergency funds here. Accessible anytime, virtually no loss.

Unit Type: Money Market Funds

  • Common products: Yu’ebao (Alipay), Lingqiantong (WeChat Pay), money market mutual funds
  • Definition: You lend money to banks and the government for a tiny amount of interest
  • Holdings: Entirely bank deposits and central bank bills — zero stocks, zero bonds
  • Annualized return: 1.2% ~ 1.6%
  • Maximum drawdown: Less than 0.1%, essentially zero

⚠️ Note: Most money market funds have a daily instant redemption cap of CNY 10,000. If you need more than that in cash urgently, do not wait until the day you need it to redeem — otherwise you may only get CNY 10,000 out.

The Core Logic of the Supply Corps

The Supply Corps is not about making money at all. Its value lies in:

  1. Emergency access: If something happens and you need cash, regular fund redemptions take 1–3 days, but the Supply Corps settles instantly
  2. Frontline reinforcement: When the Shock Troops are crashing, the Supply Corps can deploy reinforcements — continuously sending supplies to the front so you can keep buying at lower prices

Second Army: Imperial Guard (50% ~ 70% Allocation)

The bulk of your portfolio goes here. Role: park 1–3 years of idle cash, tolerate minor losses.

The Imperial Guard has two main branches: Pure Bond Funds and Fixed Income+.

2.1 Pure Bond Funds (Pure-Blood Imperial Guard)

How do you tell if a fund is a pure bond fund? Open the fund details page and check the holdings — zero stocks, zero convertible bonds means it is pure bond.

Essence: A pile of IOUs. You lend money to the government, banks, and high-quality corporations. They repay principal with interest at maturity.

Pure bond funds are divided into three categories by bond maturity:

Type Bond Maturity Annualized Return Max Drawdown Who It’s For
Short-Term Bond Fund ⭐ Under 1 year 2.5% ~ 3.5% < 1% Best for beginners
Medium/Long-Term Bond Fund 1–10 years 3% ~ 6% 1% ~ 3% Small allocation
Ultra-Long-Term Bond Fund 10+ years Extreme cases 15%+ Extreme cases -5% ~ -10% ❌ Avoid entirely

Short-Term Bond Funds (Best for Beginners)

  • Almost never lose money, more flexible than bank fixed deposits
  • With a 1-year bank fixed deposit, withdrawing early forfeits all interest. Short-term bond funds offer redeem-anytime variants with competitive returns
  • Beginners building a stable portfolio should start with short-term bond funds

Medium/Long-Term Bond Funds

  • Characteristic: better returns during rate-cut cycles. Central bank rate cuts benefit bonds; rate hikes hurt them
  • Can hold a small allocation, but should not be your core position

Ultra-Long-Term Bond Funds (❌ Stay Away)

  • During a rate-cut cycle, annual returns can surge past 15%. During a rate-hike cycle, annual losses can reach -5% to -10%
  • Volatility rivals equities. This is a battlefield where institutions deploy professional teams to track interest rate movements
  • Retail investors have no information edge — interest rate direction alone is enough to keep you guessing

2.2 Fixed Income+ (Mixed Imperial Guard)

Core logic: the main force defends the castle (bond base), while a small detachment attacks (stocks / convertible bonds) to capture some extra returns.

Type Equity Exposure Annualized Return Max Drawdown Characteristics
Primary Bond Hybrid 0% (convertible bonds only) 3.5% ~ 5.5% 2% ~ 4% The most stable entry point in Fixed Income+
Secondary Bond Hybrid ⭐ ≤ 20% 4% ~ 7% 3% ~ 6% Balanced offense/defense — what most people should focus on
Debt-Biased Hybrid ≤ 40%–50% 5% ~ 8%+ 5% ~ 10%+ Advanced tier — beginners stay away

Primary Bond Hybrid

  • Zero stocks, only bonds and convertible bonds
  • Equivalent to pure-blood Imperial Guard + a handful of convertible bond special forces
  • If you want a bit more return than pure bonds but fear volatility, start here

Secondary Bond Hybrid (⭐ Recommended)

  • 80%+ allocated to bonds, up to 20% to stocks and convertible bonds
  • When markets rally, you capture some equity upside. When markets tank, the 80% bond base keeps you afloat
  • Balanced offense and defense — no need to gamble on market direction, more stable for long-term holding

Debt-Biased Hybrid (⚠️ Beginners Stay Away)

  • Up to 40%–50% allocation to stocks
  • Rallies harder than secondary bond hybrids, crashes harder too
  • No longer really Fixed Income+ — only consider if you can accept greater volatility in pursuit of higher returns

Third Army: Shock Troops (10% ~ 40% Allocation)

⚠️ Two rules before entering:

  1. Use only idle cash you will not touch for 3–5+ years
  2. Be mentally prepared to lose it all without heartbreak — if you would feel pain, you need to reduce your position

3.1 Broad-Market Index Funds (⭐ Best for Beginners)

Definition: Track a broad market index. Buy the most representative batch of companies in the market. Earn the market’s overall returns.

  • Common indexes: CSI 300, CSI 500, ChiNext Index, Nasdaq-100, S&P 500
  • Annualized return: 8% ~ 12%
  • Maximum drawdown: 30% ~ 50%

Historical data shows that holding for 3+ years almost never results in a loss.

Why recommend broad-market indexes?

  • Poor companies eventually get eliminated from the index; only the elite remain
  • Buying the index = permanently holding the strongest group of companies in the market, earning from overall economic growth

📖 The Buffett story: In his will, Buffett instructed his wife to put 90% of her inheritance into a low-cost S&P 500 index fund.

Beginners entering the Shock Troops should start with broad-market indexes — do NOT jump into sector funds right away.

3.2 Sector / Thematic Funds (⚠️ High Risk)

Definition: Invest only in stocks of a specific sector or theme. Try to earn from sector cyclical upswings.

  • Common sectors: New energy, semiconductors, healthcare, consumer goods, defense, AI, etc.
  • Volatility: Roughly double that of broad-market indexes
  • Maximum drawdown: During sector downturns, can reach 50% ~ 70%+

Real-world case: New energy funds surged over 100% in 2021, then lost nearly half their value in 2022.

Sector funds are a bet on track logic — bet right and you win big; bet wrong and you lose big.

The threshold question — you must be able to answer:

  • Why is this sector’s cycle trending upward right now?
  • When might it reverse?

If you cannot answer these questions, you should not touch sector funds.

3.3 Equity-Biased Hybrid Funds (Actively Managed Funds)

Definition: 60%–95% allocation to stocks. Fund managers actively pick stocks and adjust the portfolio.

  • Top performers’ annualized return: 15% ~ 20%
  • Maximum drawdown: 40% ~ 60%+

⚠️ The Champion’s Curse: Throughout the history of China’s mutual fund industry, the previous year’s top-performing fund almost always suffers a massive drawdown the following year.

Why does the Champion’s Curse exist?

  1. After winning the crown, massive capital floods in and the fund’s AUM balloons by tens of times → the manager cannot find enough quality targets → excess returns get diluted
  2. The “champion” usually rode a sector tailwind that year — it does not necessarily signal genuine skill

Never buy any fund ranked in the top 10 by 1-year return. The Champion’s Curse has a 100% hit rate.

How to pick instead? Look for fund managers with 3–5+ years of track record who have weathered both bull and bear markets — the kind who consistently beat the index without relying on sector tailwinds.

3.4 QDII Funds (The Overseas Squad)

Definition: Use RMB to buy overseas funds, achieving geographic diversification.

  • Available products: Nasdaq-100, S&P 500, and other index funds
  • Annualized return: US equities 8% ~ 20%, HK equities 5% ~ 20%
  • Maximum drawdown: Varies, 20% ~ 50%+

Core purpose: Geographic diversification. When A-shares fall, you do not lose everything — the two markets do not always move in the same direction.

🚫 Iron rule: Never, ever touch crude oil funds or commodity funds!

Three Ultimate Rules to Avoid Pitfalls

Rule One: Pure Bonds Come in Three Flavors — Short Is Safe, Medium Is Okay, Ultra Is Dangerous

Short-term bond funds are the best entry point for bond investing. Medium/long-term can be a small allocation. Ultra-long-term bonds carry equity-like volatility — retail investors should stay away.

Rule Two: Beginners Should Buy Passive Funds First, Not Active Funds

Passive funds (broad-market indexes) have low fees, do not depend on any individual manager’s skill, and outperform most active funds over the long run. Only consider active funds once you have developed sufficient market judgment.

Rule Three: Funds Recommended by Banks or Apps Are Traps Nine Times Out of Ten

Platforms typically push the funds that have performed best recently — but the best performers are often the next ones to crash. Refer back to Rule Two: the Champion’s Curse spares no one.
